ma-airplane-collision-student-pilot.question: In which collisions between two airplanes was one of them flown by a student pilot?

rubric.relevant: Two or more airplanes collided (in flight or on the ground), AND the record states that one of the colliding airplanes was flown by a student pilot (solo, or a student at the controls on an instructional flight).
rubric.partial: Two airplanes collided and a student pilot or an instructional flight is mentioned, but the record does not make clear that the student was flying one of the colliding airplanes.
rubric.notRelevant: Only one aircraft was involved; or the collision was with a vehicle, an object or an animal; or neither colliding airplane was flown by a student pilot (for example, a flight review or a flight instructor flying alone).

mc-ag-arkansas-engine-after-maintenance.question: Which agricultural flights in Arkansas lost engine power within 25 flight hours of maintenance on the engine?

rubric.relevant: The record reports a loss of engine power (total or partial), AND it states maintenance on that engine (an overhaul, a repair, a part or accessory replaced or installed, or an inspection that included the engine) AND a time between that maintenance and the accident of 25 flight hours or less (in flight, tachometer or Hobbs hours, or as the first flight after it). The investigators need not link the maintenance to the power loss. A loss of engine power the pilot reported counts as reported unless the investigators dispute it.
rubric.partial: Both the power loss and engine maintenance are stated, but the time between them is given only in calendar time that does not establish 25 flight hours or less ("two weeks before"), is approximate close to the limit ("about 25 hours", "about 30 hours"), or cannot be worked out from the record.
rubric.notRelevant: No loss of engine power; or no maintenance on the engine is stated; or the stated time since that maintenance is clearly more than 25 flight hours; or the maintenance concerned only the airframe, the propeller or other systems that are not part of the engine.

edgeCases.situation: The engine had accumulated 12.4 hours since a major overhaul when it lost power.
edgeCases.why: Engine maintenance 12.4 flight hours before the power loss.

edgeCases.situation: A cylinder was replaced about 40 flight hours before the power loss.
edgeCases.why: Clearly outside the 25-hour window.

edgeCases.situation: The last annual inspection was three weeks before the accident; the hours flown since are not stated.
edgeCases.why: Calendar time only.

edgeCases.situation: The power loss happened on the first flight after the fuel control unit was replaced.
edgeCases.why: First flight after maintenance on an engine accessory.

edgeCases.situation: The engine had 15 hours since overhaul, but the airplane struck a power line and no loss of engine power is reported.
edgeCases.why: No loss of engine power.

mc-first-flight-after-annual.question: Which accidents happened on the first flight after an annual inspection?

rubric.relevant: The record states that the accident flight was the first flight after an annual inspection (or a condition inspection, its equivalent for an amateur-built or light-sport aircraft): explicitly ("the first flight since the annual"), as the test flight right after the annual, or by stating that the aircraft had not flown since the annual was completed.
rubric.partial: The accident happened shortly after an annual inspection but not on the first flight, or the record does not say it was the first (for example, 0.5 hours or one flight since the annual); or it was the first flight after a 100-hour or progressive inspection rather than an annual.
rubric.notRelevant: No recent annual inspection is described as preceding the flight, or the time since the annual is longer (several flights or days of flying); or it was the first flight after other maintenance that the record does not call an annual or condition inspection.

edgeCases.situation: The annual inspection was signed off on the morning of the accident, and the accident flight was the post-inspection test flight.
edgeCases.why: First flight after the annual.

edgeCases.situation: The airplane had flown 0.3 hours since the annual, on a test flight the day before.
edgeCases.why: Shortly after the annual, but not the first flight.

edgeCases.situation: The last annual inspection was 11 months before the accident.
edgeCases.why: Not recent.

edgeCases.situation: The accident was the first flight after the engine was replaced; no inspection is mentioned.
edgeCases.why: Other maintenance, not an annual inspection.

mc-helicopter-control-rotor-maintenance-.question: Which helicopter accidents happened within 10 flight hours after maintenance on the flight controls or rotor system?

rubric.relevant: The record states maintenance (a repair, a replacement, an adjustment or rigging, an installation, or an inspection that included the work) on a flight control component (cyclic, collective, pedals, servos, control linkages, swashplate) or a rotor system component (main or tail rotor blades, hubs, pitch links, gearboxes, drive shafts), AND that the accident happened 10 flight hours or less after it (stated in hours, or as the first flight after it). A link to the accident is not required.
rubric.partial: Such maintenance is stated, but the interval is given only in calendar time ("three days before"), is approximate near the limit ("about 10 hours"), or cannot be worked out; or a general inspection (annual, 100-hour) within 10 flight hours, without stated work on the controls or rotor system.
rubric.notRelevant: No maintenance on the flight controls or rotor system is stated; or the interval is clearly more than 10 flight hours; or the maintenance concerned only the engine, the airframe or the avionics.

edgeCases.situation: The tail rotor pitch link bearing was replaced 2.1 flight hours before the accident.
edgeCases.why: Rotor system work inside the window.

edgeCases.situation: The main rotor blades were replaced about 300 flight hours before the accident.
edgeCases.why: Clearly outside the window.

edgeCases.situation: A 100-hour inspection was done 4 flight hours before the accident; no control or rotor work is described.
edgeCases.why: A general inspection without stated control or rotor work.

edgeCases.situation: The cyclic friction was adjusted the day before; the hours flown since are not stated.
edgeCases.why: Calendar time only.

ng-carb-icing-not-conducive.question: Which airplane engine power losses happened in weather that was not conducive to carburetor icing?

rubric.relevant: The record reports a loss of engine power (total or partial), AND states that the weather conditions at the time (temperature and dew point, or the carburetor icing probability chart) were not conducive or not favorable to carburetor icing at the power setting in use. A loss of engine power the pilot reported counts as reported unless the investigators dispute it.
rubric.partial: A loss of engine power, and the record's statement about carburetor icing is mixed or qualified without saying which power setting applied (for example, conducive at glide power but not at cruise power); or the record rules out carburetor icing for a reason other than the weather (the engine was fuel injected, carburetor heat was applied).
rubric.notRelevant: No loss of engine power; or the record states the conditions were conducive to carburetor icing at the power setting in use; or carburetor icing is not discussed.

edgeCases.situation: Power loss in cruise; the temperature and dew point were "not conducive to carburetor icing at any power setting".
edgeCases.why: Explicitly not conducive.

edgeCases.situation: Power loss during the descent; "conditions were conducive to serious carburetor icing at glide power".
edgeCases.why: Conducive at the power setting in use.

edgeCases.situation: Power loss in cruise; the chart showed icing only at glide power, not at cruise power.
edgeCases.why: Not conducive at the cruise power in use.

edgeCases.situation: Power loss; the engine was fuel injected, so carburetor icing could not occur.
edgeCases.why: Icing ruled out, but not by the weather.

ng-gear-collapse-no-defect.question: Which airplane landing gear collapses happened even though no pre-existing defect was found in the gear?

rubric.relevant: A landing gear leg (main, nose or tail) collapsed, folded or retracted during the landing, takeoff or ground operation, AND the investigators state that their examination of that gear found no pre-existing defect, malfunction or anomaly (for example, "no evidence of a preimpact mechanical malfunction of the landing gear").
rubric.partial: A gear collapse, and the examination result is general or limited ("no anomalies with the airplane" without naming the gear, or the gear was not examined); or the record attributes the collapse to the landing (a hard landing, a side load, a loss of directional control) without stating an examination result.
rubric.notRelevant: No gear collapse; or the examination found a defect or failure that existed before the accident (a fatigue crack, corrosion, a failed actuator, improper rigging or maintenance); or a gear-up landing in which the gear was never extended (not a collapse).

edgeCases.situation: The nose gear collapsed after a hard landing; examination revealed no preimpact anomalies with the nose gear.
edgeCases.why: A collapse with an examination of that gear that found nothing.

edgeCases.situation: The right main gear collapsed; the trunnion had a pre-existing fatigue crack.
edgeCases.why: A pre-existing defect was found.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot forgot to extend the gear and landed gear up.
edgeCases.why: Not a collapse.

edgeCases.situation: The left main gear collapsed during a ground loop; the gear was not examined.
edgeCases.why: Collapse without an examination result.

ng-skydiving-power-loss-no-anomaly.question: Which skydiving flights lost engine power even though the engine examination afterwards found nothing mechanically wrong?

rubric.relevant: The record reports a loss of engine power (total or partial) during the flight, AND the investigators state that their examination of the engine found no mechanical malfunction, failure or anomaly (for example, "no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or anomalies that would have precluded normal operation"). Why power was lost may be undetermined or something other than an engine defect (fuel, ice, the way the engine was operated). A loss of engine power the pilot reported counts as reported unless the investigators dispute it.
rubric.partial: The record reports a loss of engine power, but leaves the examination result open: the engine was not examined, could be examined only in part (fire or impact damage), or the "no anomalies" statement covers only the airframe or only part of the engine. Also partial: the examination found nothing wrong, but the investigators doubt that power was lost.
rubric.notRelevant: No loss of engine power is reported; or the examination found an engine malfunction, failure, damage or wear that existed before the accident (for example, a fractured connecting rod, a failed magneto, a stuck valve).

edgeCases.situation: Fuel exhaustion caused the power loss, and the examination found no mechanical anomaly with the engine.
edgeCases.why: The question is about the engine's mechanical condition, not about why power was lost.

edgeCases.situation: The engine lost power on climb-out and was destroyed by the post-crash fire, so it could not be examined.
edgeCases.why: The examination result is unknown.

edgeCases.situation: The engine lost power; the examination found a fatigue fracture of the crankshaft.
edgeCases.why: A pre-existing mechanical failure was found.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported a partial loss of power; the engine later ran at full power on a test stand with no anomalies.
edgeCases.why: A reported power loss and an examination, including the test run, that found nothing wrong.

edgeCases.situation: The airplane stalled during the jump run; the engine was producing power at impact and nothing was wrong with it.
edgeCases.why: No loss of engine power.

pv-helicopter-tail-rotor-claim.question: Which helicopter accidents involved a pilot reporting a tail rotor failure that investigators did not find?

rubric.relevant: The pilot (or crew) reported a tail rotor malfunction or failure, or a loss of tail rotor control, AND the investigators found no failure or malfunction of the tail rotor system (including when they attribute the yaw to loss of tail rotor effectiveness, the flight conditions or the pilot's technique).
rubric.partial: The pilot reported a tail rotor problem and the record does not settle it (the system could not be examined, or impact damage prevented a determination).
rubric.notRelevant: The investigation found a failure or malfunction of the tail rotor system; or the pilot did not report a tail rotor problem.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported a tail rotor failure; examination established tail rotor drive continuity and the investigators attributed the spin to loss of tail rotor effectiveness.
edgeCases.why: Reported failure not found.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported a loss of tail rotor control; the tail rotor drive shaft had fractured from fatigue.
edgeCases.why: A failure was found.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported the pedals became ineffective; the tail boom was destroyed and continuity could not be established.
edgeCases.why: Not settled.

pv-pilot-reported-failure-not-confirmed.question: In which accidents did the pilot report a mechanical failure that the investigation did not confirm?

rubric.relevant: The record gives the pilot's (or another crew member's) report that a specific mechanical problem occurred (for example, a loss of engine power, a brake failure, jammed controls, a landing gear or instrument malfunction), AND the investigators state that examination or testing found no evidence of that problem, or found the system working.
rubric.partial: The pilot reported a mechanical problem, and the investigators could not examine it or leave it unresolved without saying whether evidence was found; or the investigators found a different problem without addressing the one the pilot reported.
rubric.notRelevant: The investigation confirmed the problem the pilot reported; or no crew member reported a mechanical problem (reports only by witnesses, mechanics or operators do not count).

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported that the brakes failed; examination found that the brake system operated normally.
edgeCases.why: Reported failure, examination found it working.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported a total loss of engine power; the engine test-ran without anomalies.
edgeCases.why: Reported failure not confirmed.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported a loss of engine power; examination found a failed magneto.
edgeCases.why: The investigation confirmed a failure.

edgeCases.situation: A witness reported the engine sputtering; the pilot reported no problem.
edgeCases.why: No crew report of a mechanical problem.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported that the landing gear would not extend; the gear system was not examined.
edgeCases.why: Reported problem left unresolved.

pv-recorded-data-contradicts-pilot.question: Which accidents had a pilot's account of the flight that recorded data, such as GPS or engine monitor data, contradicted?

rubric.relevant: The record states what the pilot (or crew) reported about the flight (altitude, airspeed, fuel state, engine behavior, flight path or the sequence of events) AND that data recorded by a device (GPS, ADS-B or radar data, an engine monitor, a flight data recorder, video) showed something different.
rubric.partial: The pilot's account and the recorded data differ, but the record does not point out the difference; or the pilot's account is contradicted by a witness or by physical evidence rather than by recorded data.
rubric.notRelevant: No recorded data is described; or the recorded data agree with the pilot's account; or the record gives no account by the pilot.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot said he climbed to 3,000 ft; ADS-B data showed the airplane never exceeded 900 ft.
edgeCases.why: Recorded data contradict the account.

edgeCases.situation: The pilot reported a loss of engine power; engine monitor data showed normal engine parameters until impact.
edgeCases.why: Recorded data contradict the account.

edgeCases.situation: A witness saw the airplane flying lower than the pilot reported.
edgeCases.why: Contradicted by a witness, not by recorded data.

edgeCases.situation: GPS data matched the pilot's description of the approach.
edgeCases.why: No contradiction.

SYN21LA101.factual:
The commercial pilot was flying the airplane on a skydiving flight with four parachutists on board. The pilot reported that, during the climb through about 1,500 ft above ground level, the engine lost total power. He turned back toward the airport and landed in a plowed field short of the runway, where the airplane nosed over.

Postaccident examination of the engine revealed no mechanical malfunctions or anomalies that would have precluded normal operation. The fuel tanks contained about 20 gallons of fuel.
SYN21LA101.analysis: The pilot reported a total loss of engine power during the climb. The postaccident examination of the engine did not reveal any mechanical malfunctions or anomalies that would have precluded normal operation, and the reason for the loss of power could not be determined.
SYN21LA101.probableCause: A total loss of engine power during the initial climb for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination did not reveal any anomalies.

SYN19LA111.factual:
The private pilot was on a cross-country personal flight. While in cruise flight at 4,500 ft, the engine began to run rough and lost partial power. He was unable to restore power and made a forced landing in a pasture, during which the left wing struck a fence post.

The engine was examined after the accident and no mechanical anomalies were found.
SYN19LA111.analysis: The temperature and dew point recorded near the time of the accident were not conducive to carburetor icing at any power setting. The reason for the partial loss of engine power could not be determined.
SYN19LA111.probableCause: A partial loss of engine power during cruise flight for reasons that could not be determined.

SYN19LA112.factual:

The engine was examined after the accident and no mechanical anomalies were found.
SYN19LA112.analysis: The temperature and dew point recorded near the time of the accident were conducive to serious carburetor icing at glide and descent power. It is likely that carburetor ice formed during the descent.
SYN19LA112.probableCause: A partial loss of engine power during the descent due to carburetor icing.

SYN19LA113.factual:

SYN19LA113.analysis: The temperature and dew point recorded near the time of the accident were conducive to serious carburetor icing at glide power but not at cruise power. The partial loss of power occurred in cruise flight, and its reason could not be determined.
SYN19LA113.probableCause: A partial loss of engine power during cruise flight for reasons that could not be determined.

SYN16LA121.analysis: The pilot did not maintain the proper landing attitude during the touchdown, which resulted in a hard landing.
SYN16LA121.probableCause: The pilot's improper landing flare, which resulted in a hard landing and the collapse of the nose landing gear.

The commercial pilot was applying fungicide to a rice field. He reported that, during a turn at the end of a swath run, the engine lost power. He made a forced landing in an adjacent field, and the airplane came to rest inverted.

The pilot had flown 8 hours since his most recent flight review. According to the maintenance records, the engine had last been overhauled 1,310 hours before the accident, and no engine maintenance had been performed since its last 100-hour inspection 90 hours before the accident.

Examination of the engine did not reveal any anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
SYN20LA136.analysis: The pilot reported a loss of engine power during the application flight. The airplane had been flown 8 hours since the pilot's flight review. The reason for the loss of engine power could not be determined.
SYN20LA136.probableCause: A loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined.

SYN18LA141.factual:
The private pilot departed for a local flight. Shortly after takeoff the airplane's airspeed indicator showed no indication, and the pilot returned to land with a tailwind; the airplane overran the end of the runway and struck a fence.

The airplane's annual inspection was signed off by the mechanic on the morning of the accident, and the accident flight was the first flight after the inspection. During the inspection the mechanic had disconnected the pitot line to replace the airspeed indicator.

Examination of the pitot system revealed that the pitot line was disconnected at a fitting behind the instrument panel.
SYN18LA141.analysis: The pitot line had not been reconnected after it was disconnected, which resulted in the loss of airspeed indication.
SYN18LA141.probableCause: The disconnected pitot line, which resulted in a loss of airspeed indication, and the pilot's decision to land with a tailwind, which resulted in a runway overrun.

SYN17LA151.factual:
The pilot reported that, while maneuvering at low altitude, the helicopter began a slow yaw to the right that he could not stop with the pedals. He entered an autorotation and landed hard in a field.

The tail rotor pitch link bearings had been replaced 2.1 flight hours before the accident.

Examination of the tail rotor system found the tail rotor drive and flight controls continuous; no anomalies were found.
SYN17LA151.analysis: The pilot likely did not apply sufficient pedal input in the left crosswind, which resulted in a loss of tail rotor effectiveness.
SYN17LA151.probableCause: The pilot's inadequate pedal input in a crosswind, which resulted in a loss of tail rotor effectiveness.

SYN15LA161.factual:
The pilot reported that, during the landing roll, the left brake failed and the airplane veered to the left. The airplane departed the left side of the runway and struck a taxiway sign.

Examination of the brake system after the accident found that both brakes operated normally, with no leaks in the hydraulic lines and pads within limits.
SYN15LA161.analysis: The pilot did not maintain directional control during the landing roll.
SYN15LA161.probableCause: The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll.

SYN15LA162.analysis: The pilot did not maintain directional control during the landing roll.
SYN15LA162.probableCause: The loss of left brake effectiveness due to a chafed brake hydraulic line, which resulted in a loss of directional control.

SYN14LA171.factual:
The pilot reported that, during the approach to a helipad, "the tail rotor failed" and the helicopter began to spin to the right. The helicopter descended in the spin and impacted terrain.

Examination of the tail rotor drive system established continuity from the main transmission to the tail rotor gearbox, and the tail rotor blades showed no evidence of rotation at impact consistent with a drive failure. The investigation attributed the spin to a loss of tail rotor effectiveness in the tailwind.
SYN14LA171.analysis: The approach was made with a left quartering tailwind of about 12 knots.
SYN14LA171.probableCause: The pilot's failure to maintain yaw control in a left quartering tailwind, which resulted in a loss of tail rotor effectiveness.

SYN14LA172.analysis: The approach was made with a left quartering tailwind of about 12 knots.
